newsitem.title: UK: Dlr/mark rises to day's high in quiet late Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/mark rises to day's high in quiet late Europe.

text.p: The dollar firmed to its session high against the mark by late European trade, its sentiment boosted by a forecast by Germamy's six leading economic institutions that the dollar will average 1.80 marks in 1998.
Meanwhile, it drifted in a small range against the yen, with market operators sitting tight amid a lack of new factors and the meeting of G7 finance ministers looming this weekend.

"The (German institutions') forecast provided a catalyst for the dollar today, but there is still a lot of apprehension ahead of the G7 meeting," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered here.
The dollar was at 1.7124/34 marks at 1522 GMT, just off its session high and up from 1.7034/41 in late European trade on Monday. Against the yen, it was at 126.17/27 compared with Monday's 125.58/63.

"Things were very quiet today except for the dollar/mark forecasts which caught the market short, they were enough to squeeze some short positions that were in the market," said one trader at a Japanese bank here.
The dollar's rise gained momentum in late European trade when stop-loss buying was triggered just below 1.71 marks, traders said.
French President Jacques Chirac's decision to hold a snap general election in May-June, announced on Monday, did not have much impact on the dollar.
This was understandable given that the key point of interest in this election was the implications for France's participation in European monetary union, economists said.
Action over the election focused on the mark/French franc rate, with a bit of the franc's weakness there spilling over into the dollar/franc rate, traders said.
The dollar was at 5.7800/10 French francs at 1530 GMT against 5.7484/07 late on Monday.

Although the franc was regaining some composure, fears of a victory by France's opposition would keep the currency fragile as a Socialist-led alliance would have difficulty balancing pro-EMU policies with attempts to boost the economy, economists said.

Meanwhile, renewed worries about monetary union were likely to cap the dollar against the mark in the near term, they said. The market was awaiting the release on Wednesday of the European Commission's 1997/98 forecasts for EU economies, which cover inflation, budget deficits, debt levels and GDP.
However, dollar sentiment was still seen as basically firm.

"To a large extent, the dollar's recent softness against the mark is the result of some external factors, i.e. the mark crosses. In a sense, dollar/mark is being artificially held lower," Standard Chartered's Fox said.

The British pound was firmer against the mark and dollar, boosted by attractively high British interest rates and demand for cable out of the U.S. Sterling was at 2.8035/45 marks and $1.6360/67 against late Monday's 2.7819/29 and $1.6348/58.
